plain_english: Think about the goals you set for yourself at the start. Which ones did you achieve? Which ones did you fail at? Notice how remembering your successes makes you feel good, while thinking about your failures brings pain. If you can, go back and work on the things where you failed. We must not back down when we're fighting the most important battle. We have to be willing to take hits. This fight isn't like wrestling or mixed martial arts, where winners and losers might both show great skill or little skill, and might be very lucky or very unlucky. This fight is for good fortune and happiness itself. So what if you've given up on this contest before? No one stops you from jumping back in. You don't have to wait four years for the next Olympics. As soon as you've recovered and gotten your strength back, and you bring the same energy, you can fight again. If you quit again, you can start again. If you finally win, you're like someone who never quit at all. Just don't make quitting a habit that you start to enjoy. Don't be like a bad athlete who gets beaten at every competition and slinks around like a coward.
original_excerpt: Consider as to the things which you proposed to yourself at first, which you have secured, and which you have not; and how you are pleased when you recall to memory the one, and are pained about the other; and if it is possible, recover the things wherein you failed. For we must not shrink when we are engaged in the greatest combat, but we must even take blows. For the combat before us is not in wrestling and the Pancration, in which both the successful and the unsuccessful may have the greatest merit, or may have little, and in truth may be very fortunate or very unfortunate; but the combat is for good fortune and happiness themselves. Well then, even if we have renounced the contest in this matter (for good fortune and happiness), no man hinders us from renewing the combat again, and we are not compelled to wait for another four years that the games at Olympia may come again; but as soon as you have recovered and restored yourself, and employ the same zeal, you may renew the combat again; and if again you renounce it, you may again renew it; and if you once gain the victory, you are like him who has never renounced the combat. Only do not through a habit of doing the same thing (renouncing the combat), begin to do it with pleasure, and then like a bad athlete go about after being conquered in all the circuit of the games like quails who have run away.
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Fall Off (desist) from Their Purpose, Section 1
